newsitem.title: JAPAN: Platinum, palladium prices rise sharply in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Platinum, palladium prices rise sharply in Asia.

text.p: Platinum and palladium prices rose sharply in Asia on Monday, extending gains marked in New York on Friday, buoyed by extreme tightness in the spot Zurich market amid a lack of Russian sales, traders said on Monday.

Japanese private investors also exerted upward pressure as they started covering large short positions in the Tokyo yen-based futures market, especially in palladium futures, taking advantage of the yen's rise against the dollar.

Not only the weaker dollar, which pushes down the price of imported products into Japan, but also stronger dollar-based platinum and palladium prices, prompted private investors to cover their shorts, said an analyst at a commodity broker.
Spot palladium prices broke above $170 per ounce on Monday, the highest level since April 1995.
Palladium was quoted at $170.75/171.75 per ounce at 0745 GMT, up from Friday's London fix of $164.50.
Spot platinum perked up to $396.25/75 per ounce in late Asian trade, up from around $390 in New York on Friday.
Private investors trading on TOCOM held short positions equal to about 50 tonnes of palladium as of late last week, traders said.
Japanese trading houses have been holding long positions on TOCOM and have been forced to borrow in the spot Zurich market.

On Monday in Asian trade, palladium short-term lease rates briefly jumped above 20 percent from about 10 percent a week ago, while platinum lease rates were quoted at around 18 percent, up from about 10 percent last week.

"The spot Zurich market has been extremely tight, as some overseas market players appear to be trying to intentionally squeeze the market by holding back supplies," one precious metal industry source said.
The recent spike spike in lease rates has put Japanese trade houses in a financially difficult situation, traders said.

Some market players believe the supply shortage stemming from the suspension of Russian sales since last December, would not be immediately resolved even if Russia resumes metal sales soon, as widely expected.
One industry source said Russia would need to sell a massive amount of metal in the spot market for supply tightness to ease.
Russia's platinum group metals (PGM) export agency said late last week that exports of platinum and palladium were expected to resume in about two weeks.
"We are experiencing an abnormal situation. There is nothing we can do but wait until Russia resumes sales," a precious metal trader said.
High price levels in recent months has cooled Japanese physical demand, palladium especially, traders said.
